uncited: The method takes a set of training images (low-resolution or high-resolution) and their corresponding camera poses as input.
It outputs a differentiable scene representation that can render novel views via volumetric rendering.
The core output of the query function is the volume density $\sigma$ and the emitted radiance $\mathbf{c} = \{r, g, b\}$ for a given 3D position $\mathbf{p}$ and viewing direction.
The scene representation $P_s$ consists of four 2D feature planes, each with dimensions $N \times N \times C$ (or $N_{dir} \times N_{dir} \times C$ for the directional plane).
**Positional Planes:** Three planes $P_{xy}, P_{xz}, P_{yz}$ aligned with the coordinate axes.
**View-Direction Plane:** One plane $P_{dir}$ representing the spherical coordinate space of viewing directions.
It has size $N_{dir} \times N_{dir} \times C$.
**Positional Feature Retrieval:** For a query point $\mathbf{p} = (x, y, z)$, project $\mathbf{p}$ onto the three positional planes to get 2D coordinates $(x, y)$, $(x, z)$, and $(y, z)$.
Retrieve the feature vectors $v_{xy}, v_{xz}, v_{yz}$ from $P_{xy}, P_{xz}, P_{yz}$ respectively using bilinear interpolation.
**Directional Feature Retrieval:** Compute the viewing direction $(\theta_p, \phi_p)$ (azimuth and elevation) for the ray passing through $\mathbf{p}$.
Project this direction onto $P_{dir}$ to get 2D coordinates corresponding to $(\theta_p, \phi_p)$.
**Density Prediction:** Feed $v_p$ into the coarse density decoder $D_c$ and the fine density decoder $D_f$ to obtain density values $\sigma_c$ and $\sigma_f$.
**Radiance Prediction:** Concatenate all four feature vectors ($v_{xy}, v_{xz}, v_{yz}, v_{dir}$) to form the input vector $v_{all}$.
**Volumetric Rendering:** Use the predicted $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{c}$ values along sampled rays to compute pixel colors via standard volumetric rendering equations [Parent].
*   **View-Direction Dependency:** Omitting $P_{dir}$ significantly degrades performance, especially for shiny/reflective objects with non-uniform lighting.
*   **Plane Resolution:** Using $N$ too small prohibits high-frequency representation.
*   **Time Complexity:** Query time is dominated by bilinear interpolation on four planes and a small MLP inference.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Memory usage is proportional to $4 \times N^2 \times C$.
*   **Scaling:** The representation scales well with scene size by increasing $N$, but is limited by the resolution of the training images.

The method builds on the feature plane representation proposed by Chan et al. [9] for human faces and extends it to general scenes by adding a view-direction plane and using coarse/fine decoders inspired by NeRF [32].
It aims to bridge the gap between neural rendering and 2D image super-resolution, allowing for efficient upscaling of 3D scenes from low-resolution inputs.

Set smaller than $N$ (e.g., $N_{dir}=32$) because each pixel's information is relevant to only one point on $P_{dir}$ (same viewing direction for all points on a ray), whereas it is relevant to many points on positional planes [S1, unofficial].

The claim is fully supported by the evidence in Source [S1]. Specifically, the 'Source [S1] notes' section explicitly states: 'View-direction plane resolution $N_{dir}$: Set smaller than positional planes ($N_{dir} < N$) because each pixel's information is relevant to only one point on $P_{dir}$ (same viewing direction for all points on a ray), whereas it is relevant to many points on positional planes.' Additionally, the 'Source [S1] passages' section confirms the specific values ($N=200$, $N_{dir}=32$) and reiterates the reasoning: 'Note also that we choose a smaller resolution value $N_{dir} < N$ for the view-direction feature plane $P_{dir}$... Each image pixel carries information relevant to all points along its corresponding ray r which, in turn, makes it relevant to many different locations on the positional feature planes... In contrast, all points along a ray correspond to the same viewing direction, meaning that the information in each pixel is relevant to a single point on $P_{dir}$.'
